overall_summary: Exoplanet extremes and first-person hypothetical space survival scenarios ('What If You Fell Into...') consistently drive top-tier viewership (800-1,000+ views) and superior engagement (3.5%+ like rates). Conversely, cognitive psychology facts and generic brain trivia dramatically underperform, rarely crossing 100 views.

winning_patterns.pattern: First-Person Extreme Space Survival ('What If You Fell Into...')
winning_patterns.evidence: 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (1,029 views, 38 likes) and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (972 views, 18 likes) outperformed average channel views by over 400%.
winning_patterns.action: Produce high-stakes immersive 'What If' scenarios placing the viewer directly onto terrifying cosmic anomalies or extreme planetary environments.

winning_patterns.pattern: Exotic Planetary Phenomena & Counter-Intuitive Space Realities
winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' (1,030 views, 36 likes) and 'Venus Has a Day Longer Than Its Year' (981 views, 21 likes) generated the strongest organic retention and reach.
winning_patterns.action: Focus on named exoplanets or planetary anomalies with striking visual contradictions (e.g., worlds of iron snow, molten glass, or crushing gravitational physics).

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5 to 53 views across three attempts) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) showed near-zero viewer retention and algorithmic pick-up.
weak_patterns.action: Cease low-stakes brain trivia and psychology micro-facts; prioritize visual spectacle, existential mystery, or cinematic environmental tension.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Octopuses Have THREE Hearts' (12s, 0-1 likes despite multiple re-uploads) and 'The Only Animal That Can Live Forever' (69 views, 0 likes) fail to provoke deep engagement.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid standard textbook biology facts; if covering animals, frame through high-stakes cinematic survival stories rather than static anatomical trivia.

next_video.hook_style: Second-person existential threat / visceral sensory hook
next_video.concept: What would happen if an astronaut descended into the clouds of WASP-76b, the rogue gas giant where nights rain vaporized liquid iron from 4,000-degree winds?
next_video.opening_direction: Instant POV descent showing a spacesuit visor reflecting glowing orange skies: 'If you fell into WASP-76b, your suit wouldn't burn—it would melt from liquid iron rain.'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the daytime side is hot enough to vaporize rock into atmospheric gas, while the 10,000 mph wind currents condense it into supersonic molten shrapnel on the dark side.
next_video.reason: Leverages the proven high-converting 'What If You Fell Into' framework and space anomaly fascination while presenting a completely fresh entity not yet featured in channel history.
fresh_topic_constraints: Do not reuse TrES-2b, 55 Cancri e, burning ice (Gliese 436b), or Saturn ring comparisons
Must focus specifically on WASP-76b atmospheric horror and iron condensation dynamics

experiment: Test shifting hook delivery from third-person descriptive ('This planet rains...') to immediate second-person sensory dread ('If your helmet cracked here...') to test whether viewer retention past 3 seconds increases like-to-view ratio above 4.0%.
